body.text: The diplomatic and energy blockade imposed by U.S. President Donald Trump has confronted Cuba’s post-Castro regime with one of the greatest challenges to its survival. The capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in January 2026, the disruption of Venezuelan oil supplies, and mounting pressure on Mexico have further weakened Havana’s position. Meanwhile, the ideological realignment of several Latin American governments toward Washington has narrowed Cuba’s regional network of political allies, deepening its diplomatic and economic isolation.

Against this backdrop, Havana appears to be turning toward its longstanding communist allies in Asia. Countries such as China, Vietnam, and North Korea offer more than diplomatic support against U.S. pressure. Despite their considerable economic and institutional differences, these countries represent distinct experiences of one-party regime survival, sharing a commitment to preserving the political monopoly of their respective communist parties.

Developments documented by the authoritarian cooperation monitoring project of Gobierno y Análisis Político (GAPAC) during September and October 2026 illustrate this convergence. Yet they also raise a fundamental contradiction: How far is Cuba willing to reform its economy if the changes required to ensure its survival could ultimately challenge the political structures the regime seeks to preserve?
The Paths of Asian Communism

The Chinese and Vietnamese experiences offer an unavoidable contrast with Cuba’s economic trajectory. Since the reforms initiated by Deng Xiaoping in 1978 and Vietnam’s Đổi Mới process launched in 1986, both countries have developed economic models that substantially expanded the role of markets, private investment, and international trade without relinquishing the political monopoly of their respective communist parties.

As economist Carmelo Mesa-Lago has noted, the differences between the Chinese and Vietnamese economic models and Cuba’s are substantial. While the former have allowed greater decentralization and private sector participation, Havana continues to favor central planning, accompanied by partial and inconsistent reforms.

These are, of course, not identical experiences. China and Vietnam differ in their productive structures, levels of development, and integration into the international economy. Moreover, in both countries economic growth has not resulted in the democratization of the political system. Precisely for this reason, their experiences appeal to a Cuban leadership interested in identifying mechanisms of economic modernization compatible with the survival of its own regime.

A particularly illustrative development took place on September 24, when a delegation from Cuba’s Ministry of Justice, headed by Olga Lidia Pérez Díaz, held exchanges in Hanoi to learn about Vietnam’s experience in adapting its legal framework to economic transformation. Discussions addressed the regulation of relations between state-owned and private enterprises, as well as greater decentralization and autonomy for the former.

This episode is significant because it demonstrates that cooperation between the two countries extends beyond declarations of solidarity. It also encompasses mechanisms of institutional learning through which Cuba seeks to understand economic reform experiences within a political system that preserves the ruling party’s supremacy.

Nevertheless, there is a considerable gap between studying the Vietnamese model and being willing to replicate its transformations. After decades of gradual reform, the Cuban leadership remains reluctant to deepen market-oriented mechanisms capable of altering existing patterns of ownership, production, and resource distribution. In this sense, institutional learning appears to unfold within boundaries defined by the preservation of the prevailing political order.
China and the “Construction of Socialism”

Cuba’s relations with China reveal another dimension of Havana’s Asia strategy. On September 23, Beijing sent Cuba 200 containers of solar power systems, intended for homes and public institutions in remote areas. The transfer represents China’s tangible contribution to alleviating the energy crisis gripping the island.

Yet Chinese cooperation extends beyond its economic implications. During commemorations marking the anniversary of bilateral diplomatic relations, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun reaffirmed Beijing’s support for Cuba’s “construction of socialism suited to its national conditions.”

This formulation carries considerable political significance. Much like the self-described “socialism with Chinese characteristics,” the Cuban model invokes its supposedly distinctive national circumstances to justify preserving concentrated structures of political power. In the name of pursuing their own development path, both Cuba and China reject principles such as liberal democracy and universal human rights, often portrayed in official discourse as foreign, Western impositions. Beijing’s support thus extends to the legitimization of Cuba’s political system, despite the profound economic differences between the two countries.

However, ideological solidarity has not prevented significant economic tensions from emerging between the two governments, particularly over the market reforms Beijing considers necessary to sustain its commercial relationship with Havana. In October 2024, for example, a Financial Times investigation revealed growing frustration among Chinese officials and business executives with the Cuban regime’s reluctance to undertake far-reaching economic reforms. The deterioration of bilateral trade, compounded by Havana’s unpaid debts, had led to the cancellation of a contract under which China purchased more than 400,000 tons of Cuban sugar annually, as the island’s collapsing productive capacity made it unable to fulfill its commitments.

This episode exposes an unavoidable difficulty. While Beijing publicly defends Cuba’s right to develop a political and economic model suited to its national circumstances, its own commercial relations reveal the limits of Havana’s system. Ideological affinity, after all, does not guarantee that allies will indefinitely finance the inefficiencies of the Cuban economy.
Ideology as an Instrument of Survival

Cuba’s cooperation with Asia also encompasses mechanisms of ideological legitimation. On September 18, the Vietnam Academy of Social Sciences and the Cuban Embassy organized a seminar in Hanoi on Fidel Castro’s political thought, as part of the commemorations marking the centenary of his birth. The event brought together academics and officials from both countries to discuss the continued relevance of Castro’s political legacy and its contribution to bilateral relations.

The meeting is revealing in how it connects the historical memory of the Cuban and Vietnamese revolutions with contemporary efforts at political cooperation. Castro continues to serve as a source of political legitimacy, allowing the survival of both one-party systems to be presented as expressions of a shared revolutionary tradition, despite their divergent economic trajectories.

A similar expression of ideological solidarity emerged in relations with North Korea. On October 10, Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez congratulated the Workers’ Party of Korea on its anniversary, highlighting its role in building socialism and defending national sovereignty. Unlike China and Vietnam, North Korea offers few useful models of economic modernization. Its significance for Havana lies primarily in ideological affinity and the continuity of political relations between governments that uphold one-party socialism. Laos, meanwhile, maintains institutional exchanges with Cuba, albeit on a considerably smaller scale.

The differences between these countries’ economies, priorities, and international capabilities are far too substantial to allow the emergence of a true communist bloc. Nevertheless, they reveal a political community built around shared historical references, where Cuba seeks diplomatic support, resources, and governing experience from its Asian partners.
Reforming to Survive

The paradox of Cuba’s rapprochement with its Asian communist allies is that the development models most appealing to Havana have involved far more profound economic transformations than anything undertaken on the island. The post-Castro leadership seeks the benefits of the Chinese and Vietnamese experiences – economic growth, foreign investment, and greater productive capacity – without necessarily embracing the institutional changes that made them possible. Although economic liberalization does not automatically lead to democratization, as both China and Vietnam have proved, the emergence of new economic actors, private interests, and spaces of social autonomy could challenge established power structures in Cuba.

Cuba’s Asian rapprochement thus serves a dual purpose: securing material support amid growing international pressure while reaffirming the legitimacy of its one-party political system. Yet the principal obstacles to this strategy appear to lie within Cuba itself. China and Vietnam have demonstrated that far-reaching economic reforms can coexist with authoritarian political structures, but Havana continues to resist comparable transformations despite its growing dependence on external assistance.

Perhaps the greatest contradiction of Cuban communism is that its survival increasingly depends on reforms its own leaders appear reluctant to undertake. As Havana looks to Asia for ways to prolong the life of its revolution, it faces a question its allies began addressing decades ago: Can communism survive without fundamentally transforming the economy meant to sustain it?
